newsitem.title: NORWAY: FOCUS-Hydro shares tumble on 1996 results.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hydro shares tumble on 1996 results.

text.p: Shares in Norway's largest listed company Norsk Hydro ASA slumped on Monday after it blamed lower earnings from petrochemicals and metals for a 10 percent drop in 1996 operating profit.

Hydro posted an operating result of 9.65 billion crowns ($1.4 billion) for 1996 compared with 10.70 billion a year ago. Pre-tax profits were down seven percent at 10.28 billion crowns versus 11.09 billion crowns.
The result included a charge of one billion crowns due to a downward revision of remaining oil and gas reserves in the North Sea Frigg area and for provisions for future abandonment costs.

Net profits of 6.20 billion crowns, against 7.15 billion, included a reduction in the provision for deferred taxes of 776 million crowns due to a change in the tax law for hydroelectric power plants in Norway.
"Excluding the effect of the change in tax law, net income would have been 5,428 million (crowns). This was a decline of 24 percent compared with 1995," the company said in a statement.
"The reduction was principally due to lower prices for aluminium and petrochemical products, and a decrease in energy production."
The figures were more than a billion crowns below analysts' expectations on an operating level. Hydro's share price on the Oslo bourse plunged 28.50 to 350 crowns.
"The results are appallingly bad both on the underlying performance and per division," said one London-based analyst.

Net income in the fourth quarter was 2.01 billion crowns, including the deferred tax effect of the change in the tax law. Excluding the tax effect, net income was 1.24 billion crowns, down 10 percent from the fourth quarter 1995, Hydro said.

It said fourth-quarter fertiliser earnings sank 26 percent to 386 million crowns against 521 million crowns in the corresponding year-ago period. Operating profit for agriculture for the year was 2.67 billion crowns.

"In the fertiliser area we had a somewhat weaker fourth quarter than anticipated," Georg Stoermer, Hydro's Chief Financial Officer (CFO), said in an interview with Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
"The reason for that is that there has been slow volume in the fourth quarter, but I don't think it is indicative of what will happen over a whole year," he said.
Stoermer said the outlook for 1997 was difficult but he expected 1997 net profits to be on par with 1996.

"I think the best guess is that it will not be all that different (from 1996)," he said. "Particularly on the net profit level, because we have a high tax rate on petroleum, and petroleum earnings do not mean as much as earnings in the other areas in terms of the net effect."

Operating profits for oil and gas, including the Frigg writedown, jumped 72 percent to 5.63 billion crowns, versus 3.28 billion crowns, due to higher crude and gas prices, increased production and improved earnings in refining and marketing.

Hydro said a fall in aluminium prices, weaker results from semi-fabricating activities and aluminium trading, and lower electricity production were responsible for operating profits in the light metals division plunging to 1.25 billion crowns compared with 3.66 billion crowns in 1995.

Higher maintenance costs and lower prices for vinylchloride monomer (VCM), polyvinylchloride (PVC) and caustic soda had a negative impact on petrochemicals operating profits, which fell to 287 million crowns from 1.14 billion crowns.

Hydro president and chief executive officer Egil Myklebust said in the company's Profile newsletter that 1995 and 1996 results were in line with the Hydro Plus programme launched in 1993 to increase operating income to 10 billion crowns.

"On the other hand, the impact made by market fluctuations on the 1996 result shows us that we still need to improve our cost efficiency. Our fourth-quarter results are a reminder of that," Myklebust said. ($1 = 6.676 Norwegian Crowns)
